export const meta = {
  name: 'extron-pkp-controlscript-feasibility',
  description: 'Analyze Extron .pkp vs ControlScript .py across 9 dimensions, adversarially verify, synthesize a two-direction feasibility verdict',
  phases: [
    { title: 'Analyze', detail: '9 parallel dimension analysts over the sample pairs' },
    { title: 'Verify', detail: 'adversarial skeptic per dimension, re-checking claims against the files' },
    { title: 'Synthesize', detail: 'per-direction verdicts + completeness critic' },
  ],
}

const ROOT = '/Users/robp/GitHub/rob-paprocki/extron-driver-convert'

const GROUND = `
GROUND TRUTH ALREADY ESTABLISHED (do not re-derive, but DO challenge if you find contradicting evidence):

- An Extron .pkp file is gzip-compressed. Decompressed, it is a .NET BinaryFormatter
  serialization stream (NRBF / [MS-NRBF]), starting with the SerializationHeaderRecord
  bytes 00 01 00 00 00 FF FF FF FF 01 00 00 00 00 00 00 00.
- Its BinaryLibrary records name assemblies: Extron.Configuration.Drivers,
  Extron.Configuration.Contracts, Extron.Configuration.Core, all Version=13.26.0.15.
- Types present include: DriverModelAsset, DriverCommandAsset, DriverFileAsset,
  EnumParamAsset, DecimalParamAsset, StringParamAsset, EnumStateAsset,
  EthernetProtocolAsset, DanteAsset, StreamResourceAsset, RevisionHistoryAsset,
  UTF8Password, and enums such as ExtronCommandIdEnum, DriverAttributeEnum,
  ParamAttributeFlags, OperatorFlags, ProtocolCompatibilityFlags,
  DriverConditionTypeFlags, EthernetTypeEnum, HTTPAuthenticationSchemesEnum,
  CertificationEnum, DanteNicEnum, DriverPackageStateEnum.
- There is NO encryption and NO code signing on the container.
- Each .pkp embeds a COMPLETE Python driver source targeting the Global Configurator
  runtime: 'from Extron2.BaseDriver import BaseDriver', 'import Extron.Timer as
  CallBackTimer', 'from Extron import Platform, Version', and a
  'class extr_<id>(BaseDriver)'. It also defines 'class ExtronTime(float)'.
- The separately-shipped ControlScript module targets a DIFFERENT runtime:
  'from extronlib.interface import SerialInterface, EthernetClientInterface',
  'from extronlib.system import Wait, ProgramLog', 'class DeviceClass:' plus
  'class SSHClass(EthernetClientInterface, DeviceClass)' and similar transport classes.
  It carries a self.Commands dict keyed by command name with 'Parameters' and 'Status'.
- Line counts: embedded GC Python 2135 (DSC) / 2325 (DTP3); shipped ControlScript
  1238 (DSC) / 1335 (DTP3).

FILES ON DISK (absolute paths):
  Decompressed NRBF payloads (binary):
    ${ROOT}/tools/out/DSC_12G-HD.raw
    ${ROOT}/tools/out/DTP3_CP_42.raw
  Python extracted from inside the .pkp (GC runtime):
    ${ROOT}/tools/out/embedded/DSC_12G-HD.embedded.py
    ${ROOT}/tools/out/embedded/DTP3_CP_42.embedded.py
  Shipped ControlScript modules (extronlib runtime):
    ${ROOT}/samples/DSC_12G-HD/controlscript/extr_scaler_DSC_12G_HD_A_v1_0_0_0.py
    "${ROOT}/samples/DTP3 CP 42/controlscript/extr_matrix_DTP3_CrossPoint_42_Series_v1_2_0_0.py"
  Original .pkp files:
    ${ROOT}/samples/DSC_12G-HD/pkp/extr_17_17677_v1_0_0.pkp
    "${ROOT}/samples/DTP3 CP 42/pkp/extr_15_17578_v1_3_0.pkp"
  Comm sheets / driver docs (PDF):
    ${ROOT}/samples/DSC_12G-HD/pkp/extr_17_17677_v1_0_0.pdf
    ${ROOT}/samples/DSC_12G-HD/controlscript/extr_scaler_DSC_12G_HD_A_v1_0_0_0.pdf
    "${ROOT}/samples/DTP3 CP 42/pkp/extr_15_17578_v1_3_0.pdf"
    "${ROOT}/samples/DTP3 CP 42/controlscript/extr_matrix_DTP3_CrossPoint_42_Series_v1_2_0_0.pdf"
  Product manuals with SIS command tables (PDF):
    ${ROOT}/samples/DSC_12G-HD/68-3221-01_A_DSC_12G-HD_HD-12G_A_UG.pdf
    "${ROOT}/samples/DTP3 CP 42/68-3581-01_B_DTP3_CP_42_USB.pdf"

NOTE: paths containing "DTP3 CP 42" have a SPACE in them. Quote them in shell commands.
Both devices are Extron first-party products using the Extron SIS command set.

RULES:
- Every claim you make MUST cite evidence: a file path plus line number, a quoted
  code excerpt, or a byte offset. A claim you cannot cite is an open question, not a finding.
- Do not speculate about Extron software you cannot inspect. Say "unknown" instead.
- You have Bash. Use python3, grep, sed. pdftotext may or may not exist; if not, try
  'mutool draw -F txt', or python3 with pypdf/pdfminer if installed, or fall back to
  strings. Report if you could not read a PDF rather than inventing its contents.
`

const FINDINGS_SCHEMA = {
  type: 'object',
  properties: {
    dimension: { type: 'string' },
    summary: { type: 'string', description: '3-6 sentences: what you established' },
    findings: {
      type: 'array',
      items: {
        type: 'object',
        properties: {
          claim: { type: 'string' },
          evidence: { type: 'string', description: 'file:line, byte offset, or quoted excerpt' },
          confidence: { type: 'string', enum: ['high', 'medium', 'low'] },
          bearing: { type: 'string', enum: ['pkp->py', 'py->pkp', 'both', 'neither'] },
          implication: { type: 'string', description: 'what this means for convertibility' },
        },
        required: ['claim', 'evidence', 'confidence', 'bearing'],
      },
    },
    openQuestions: { type: 'array', items: { type: 'string' } },
  },
  required: ['dimension', 'summary', 'findings'],
}

const VERDICT_SCHEMA = {
  type: 'object',
  properties: {
    dimension: { type: 'string' },
    verified: {
      type: 'array',
      items: {
        type: 'object',
        properties: {
          claim: { type: 'string' },
          verdict: { type: 'string', enum: ['CONFIRMED', 'REFUTED', 'UNCERTAIN'] },
          note: { type: 'string', description: 'what you checked and what you saw' },
        },
        required: ['claim', 'verdict'],
      },
    },
    missedOrWrong: { type: 'array', items: { type: 'string' }, description: 'things the analyst got wrong or failed to look at' },
  },
  required: ['dimension', 'verified'],
}

const DIMENSIONS = [
  {
    key: 'pkp-container',
    prompt: `Fully characterize the .pkp container and BUILD A WORKING PARSER.

Write a real NRBF parser at ${ROOT}/tools/pkp_dump.py. It must: gunzip a .pkp, walk the
[MS-NRBF] record stream (SerializationHeaderRecord, BinaryLibrary, ClassWithMembersAndTypes,
SystemClassWithMembersAndTypes, ClassWithId, BinaryObjectString, BinaryArray, ArraySingleObject,
ArraySinglePrimitive, MemberReference, ObjectNull, MessageEnd, etc.), resolve object references
into a graph, and emit JSON. You are the ONLY agent permitted to write files under ${ROOT}/tools/.

Run it on BOTH .raw payloads. Write the JSON to ${ROOT}/tools/out/<device>.pkp.json.

Then report: the complete inventory of record/object types present, the top-level object graph
shape (what is the root, what hangs off it), the member names of each Extron asset class, how
many DriverCommandAsset / ParamAsset / EnumStateAsset instances exist per device, and where the
embedded Python source sits in the graph (which asset holds it, and in what member).

If any part of the stream defeats your parser, say exactly which record type and offset — a
partial parser honestly described is worth more than a complete-looking one that guessed.`,
  },
  {
    key: 'pkp-nonpython',
    prompt: `The .pkp holds structured driver metadata ALONGSIDE the embedded Python. Characterize
that metadata and determine whether it is redundant with the Python or additional to it.

Focus on: DriverCommandAsset (what fields define a command?), EnumParamAsset / DecimalParamAsset /
StringParamAsset / EnumStateAsset (how are parameters typed, ranged, enumerated?), the
ExtronCommandIdEnum values, DriverAttributeEnum / ParamAttributeFlags / OperatorFlags,
EthernetProtocolAsset and DanteAsset (connection/transport config), RevisionHistoryAsset,
StreamResourceAsset (what resources are embedded besides Python — the PDF?), UTF8Password.

The decisive question: is the structured metadata the SOURCE from which the embedded Python was
GENERATED, or is it a parallel description used by the GC UI while the Python is hand-written?
Look for generation fingerprints — a 'Created on <date>' docstring, mechanical naming, one Python
method per DriverCommandAsset, identical ordering between the metadata list and the Python. Report
which hypothesis the evidence supports and how strongly.

Use strings/grep/python3 on the .raw files. If ${ROOT}/tools/pkp_dump.py exists by the time you
run, you may use it, but do NOT write to ${ROOT}/tools/ yourself — work in /tmp.`,
  },
  {
    key: 'gc-python-anatomy',
    prompt: `Map the anatomy of the GC-runtime Python embedded in the .pkp files (the two
*.embedded.py files). Read them in full — they are ~2100-2300 lines each.

Report: the class hierarchy and what BaseDriver appears to provide (infer its API from every
attribute/method the subclass uses or overrides); how commands are declared and dispatched; how
parameters are validated; how device responses are matched and parsed; how state/subscription
callbacks work; what timers/polling exist; the transport abstraction (how does it talk serial vs
Ethernet vs SSH?); anything device-specific vs boilerplate.

Quantify the boilerplate-vs-unique split: roughly how many lines are identical framework scaffolding
shared between the two devices, versus device-specific command logic? Establish that with a real
diff, not an impression.`,
  },
  {
    key: 'cs-python-anatomy',
    prompt: `Map the anatomy of the two shipped ControlScript modules (the extronlib ones under
samples/*/controlscript/*.py). Read them in full.

Report: the class structure (DeviceClass plus the transport mixin classes — enumerate ALL of them),
the exact shape of the self.Commands dict, how Set*/Update*/Parse methods are named and generated,
how AddMatchString and the receive buffer work, how Subscription and callbacks work, error handling
and ProgramLog use, how connection state is tracked, and what extronlib API surface is required.

Then quantify the boilerplate-vs-unique split between the two device modules with a real diff, the
same way as for the GC modules. Note any evidence these files are machine-generated (ordering,
comment style, repeated idioms, a generator version stamp).`,
  },
  {
    key: 'diff-dsc',
    prompt: `THE CENTRAL QUESTION, device 1. For the DSC 12G-HD you have the SAME DRIVER in both
worlds: the GC Python embedded in the .pkp, and the shipped ControlScript module.

Do a rigorous same-device comparison:
- Enumerate the command set exposed by each. Build the two lists and diff them by name.
  Which commands exist in both? Only in the .pkp? Only in ControlScript?
- For 8-12 representative commands spanning simple/parameterised/status/enum kinds, put the two
  implementations side by side. Show the actual SIS command string each builds, the parameter
  handling, and the response-matching pattern. Are the wire strings IDENTICAL?
- Are the response regexes identical, equivalent-but-rewritten, or genuinely different?
- What does one have that the other structurally cannot express?

Deliver a concrete percentage: what fraction of the ControlScript module's behaviour is
mechanically derivable from the .pkp's contents? Justify the number.`,
  },
  {
    key: 'diff-dtp3',
    prompt: `THE CENTRAL QUESTION, device 2. Same task as the DSC comparison but for the
DTP3 CrossPoint 42 — the GC Python embedded in its .pkp vs its shipped ControlScript module.

This device is a MATRIX, so pay particular attention to how the two express matrix ties, IO naming,
per-input/output addressing, and the OrderedDict usage. Also note that the .pkp Python defines a
SUBCLASS 'extr_15_17578_usb(extr_15_17578)' for the USB variant — determine how the ControlScript
module handles the multiple supported models by comparison.

Do the same work: full command-set diff by name, 8-12 representative side-by-side implementations
with the actual SIS wire strings and response patterns, structural gaps in each direction, and a
justified percentage for how much of the ControlScript module is mechanically derivable from the .pkp.

Report specifically whether your conclusions AGREE with what a matrix-vs-scaler difference would
predict, so a second device either corroborates or breaks the single-device conclusion.`,
  },
  {
    key: 'runtime-apis',
    prompt: `Compare the two RUNTIMES the drivers target, since that gap is what any converter must
bridge. Runtime A: Extron2.BaseDriver / Extron.Timer / Extron.Platform / Extron.Version (GC).
Runtime B: extronlib.interface / extronlib.system (ControlScript).

Infer each API's surface purely from usage in the four Python files — every import, base-class
method called via super(), every attribute the subclass assumes exists, every override.

Produce a mapping table: for each GC BaseDriver facility, the extronlib equivalent, marked
1:1 / equivalent-with-rewrite / no-counterpart. Do the same in reverse. Call out specifically:
connection lifecycle, send/receive and byte encoding, response matching, timers and polling,
logging, platform/version gating, and the 'ExtronTime(float)' oddity.

State clearly which gaps are MECHANICAL (a translator could emit the right call) and which require
human judgement.`,
  },
  {
    key: 'sis-docs',
    prompt: `Evaluate the PDFs as a THIRD source of truth. Extract text from the two product manuals
and the four driver comm sheets.

Determine: does the comm sheet enumerate the same command set as the driver files, in a
machine-readable-enough form to drive or validate a conversion? Do the manuals' SIS command tables
(command string, response, description) line up with what the drivers actually send? Are there
commands in the SIS documentation that neither driver implements?

The strategic question to answer: if .pkp -> .py conversion turned out to be lossy, could the SIS
documentation fill the gap — i.e. is a doc-driven or doc-validated generator viable as a fallback
or a cross-check? Assess how consistent the PDF structure is between the two products, since a
parser would need to handle both.

If you cannot extract PDF text with the tools available, say so explicitly and report what you
tried rather than guessing at contents.`,
  },
  {
    key: 'reverse-direction',
    prompt: `Assess the REVERSE direction: ControlScript .py -> .pkp. This is the direction most
likely to be infeasible; your job is to establish exactly why, or to show it is more possible than
expected. Argue it honestly in both directions rather than assuming the answer.

Determine what a valid .pkp requires that a ControlScript module simply does not contain:
the structured asset graph, ExtronCommandIdEnum identifiers, parameter type/range/enum metadata,
GC UI-facing naming and descriptions, protocol assets, certification/revision fields, the driver
ID numbering scheme (note the .pkp filenames are extr_17_17677 and extr_15_17578 while the
ControlScript names are extr_scaler_DSC_12G_HD_A and extr_matrix_DTP3_CrossPoint_42_Series —
work out what those numbers mean and whether they are allocatable outside Extron).

Also assess mechanical feasibility of WRITING the container: NRBF is a documented format, but
re-serializing a .NET object graph that GC will load requires exact type identity, assembly version
match (13.26.0.15), and member layout. Judge how brittle that is, and whether GC validates or
rejects packages it did not produce (say 'unknown' if you cannot tell from the files).

Consider also the practical question: is there any legitimate reason to want this direction at all,
given the embedded-Python discovery? Say so if the direction is answerable but pointless.`,
  },
]

phase('Analyze')
log(`Analyzing ${DIMENSIONS.length} dimensions across 2 matched device pairs (pkp + ControlScript)`)

const analyzed = await pipeline(
  DIMENSIONS,
  (d) => agent(`${GROUND}\n\nYOUR DIMENSION: ${d.key}\n\n${d.prompt}`, {
    label: `analyze:${d.key}`,
    phase: 'Analyze',
    schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA,
    model: 'sonnet',
    effort: 'high',
  }),
  (result, d) => {
    if (!result) return null
    return agent(
      `${GROUND}\n\nYou are an adversarial verifier. Another analyst studied the dimension "${d.key}" and produced the findings below. ` +
      `Your job is to REFUTE them, not to agree with them. Open the actual files and check each claim yourself. ` +
      `Mark a claim CONFIRMED only if you personally reproduced the evidence. Mark it REFUTED if the evidence does not support it ` +
      `or contradicts it. Mark it UNCERTAIN if you could not check. Default to skepticism: a plausible-sounding claim with vague ` +
      `evidence ("the file shows...", "generally...") that you cannot pin to a specific line is NOT confirmed.\n\n` +
      `Also report anything the analyst MISSED or got backwards that materially changes the convertibility picture.\n\n` +
      `Their brief was:\n${d.prompt}\n\n` +
      `THEIR FINDINGS:\n${JSON.stringify(result, null, 2)}`,
      {
        label: `verify:${d.key}`,
        phase: 'Verify',
        schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA,
        model: 'sonnet',
        effort: 'high',
      }
    ).then((v) => ({ dimension: d.key, analysis: result, verification: v }))
  }
)

const dossier = analyzed.filter(Boolean)
const confirmedCount = dossier.reduce(
  (n, d) => n + ((d.verification && d.verification.verified) || []).filter((v) => v.verdict === 'CONFIRMED').length, 0)
const refutedCount = dossier.reduce(
  (n, d) => n + ((d.verification && d.verification.verified) || []).filter((v) => v.verdict === 'REFUTED').length, 0)
log(`${dossier.length}/${DIMENSIONS.length} dimensions complete — ${confirmedCount} claims confirmed, ${refutedCount} refuted`)

phase('Synthesize')
const EVIDENCE = JSON.stringify(dossier, null, 2)

const [forward, reverse, critic] = await parallel([
  () => agent(
    `${GROUND}\n\nBelow is the full verified evidence dossier from 9 analysis dimensions, each adversarially checked.\n\n` +
    `Write the FEASIBILITY VERDICT for the .pkp -> ControlScript .py direction. Weight REFUTED claims as false and ` +
    `UNCERTAIN claims as unproven; build only on CONFIRMED evidence.\n\n` +
    `Cover: (1) a one-paragraph plain-English answer to "is it possible"; (2) what converts mechanically and with what fidelity; ` +
    `(3) what converts lossily and what is lost; (4) what has no counterpart and must be hand-written; (5) a concrete proposed ` +
    `architecture for a converter, given the embedded-Python discovery — including whether the right move is to translate the ` +
    `embedded GC Python, to generate from the .pkp asset metadata, or a hybrid; (6) the honest effort estimate and the top three risks; ` +
    `(7) how the conclusion would need to change for third-party (non-SIS) drivers, which are the eventual target.\n\n` +
    `Be specific and cite evidence. Prose with headings, no bullet-soup. Do not hedge where the evidence is clear, ` +
    `and do not overclaim where it is not.\n\nDOSSIER:\n${EVIDENCE}`,
    { label: 'verdict:pkp->py', phase: 'Synthesize', model: 'fable', effort: 'max' }
  ),
  () => agent(
    `${GROUND}\n\nBelow is the full verified evidence dossier from 9 analysis dimensions, each adversarially checked.\n\n` +
    `Write the FEASIBILITY VERDICT for the ControlScript .py -> .pkp direction. Weight REFUTED claims as false and ` +
    `UNCERTAIN as unproven.\n\n` +
    `Cover: (1) plain-English answer; (2) precisely what information a .pkp needs that a ControlScript module does not carry, ` +
    `and whether it can be synthesised, inferred, or must be authored; (3) the mechanical problem of writing a valid NRBF stream ` +
    `that GC will accept, and how brittle that is; (4) the driver-ID / versioning / certification obstacle; (5) whether a partial ` +
    `or "best-effort skeleton" version of this direction has any practical value; (6) an honest recommendation on whether to ` +
    `pursue it at all.\n\nBe specific and cite evidence. Prose with headings.\n\nDOSSIER:\n${EVIDENCE}`,
    { label: 'verdict:py->pkp', phase: 'Synthesize', model: 'sonnet', effort: 'high' }
  ),
  () => agent(
    `${GROUND}\n\nBelow is the full verified evidence dossier from 9 analysis dimensions.\n\n` +
    `You are the COMPLETENESS CRITIC. Do not summarise. Identify what is MISSING: which questions remain unanswered, which ` +
    `claims survived only because nobody checked them, which files or angles were never examined, and what additional sample ` +
    `files would most change the conclusions. Also flag any place where the two device pairs DISAGREE with each other, since ` +
    `a conclusion drawn from one device and contradicted by the other is not yet a conclusion.\n\n` +
    `Rank what you find by how much it would change the feasibility verdict. Be blunt.\n\nDOSSIER:\n${EVIDENCE}`,
    { label: 'completeness-critic', phase: 'Synthesize', model: 'sonnet', effort: 'high' }
  ),
])

return {
  dimensionsAnalyzed: dossier.length,
  claimsConfirmed: confirmedCount,
  claimsRefuted: refutedCount,
  dossier,
  verdictForward: forward,
  verdictReverse: reverse,
  completenessCritic: critic,
}

analysis.summary: Built a from-scratch [MS-NRBF] parser at /Users/robp/GitHub/rob-paprocki/extron-driver-convert/tools/pkp_dump.py that gunzips a .pkp (or accepts an already-decompressed .raw stream), walks the full NRBF record stream, resolves the object graph, and emits JSON. It fully parses both sample files with zero bytes left over (fully_parsed=True, bytes_consumed==decompressed_size for both). Output written to tools/out/DSC_12G-HD.pkp.json (7,074,002 bytes) and tools/out/DTP3_CP_42.pkp.json (7,474,598 bytes). The root object is a single Extron.Configuration.Drivers.DriverFileAsset; its child collection fans out through five typed per-kind registries (AssetBase`1 wrappers for IDriverCommandAsset, IDriverModelAsset, IParamAsset, IProtocolAsset, IResourceAsset) plus two RevisionHistoryAsset entries. The embedded GC Python driver source lives as raw bytes inside a StreamResourceAsset under the IResourceAsset registry, keyed by filename. Three .NET/BCL wire shapes needed hand-coded support because NRBF's untyped class records carry no per-member type info (real .NET resolves it via CLR reflection): enum instances, System.Guid, System.Version, List`1 (mixed raw+record fields), and ObservableCollection`1+SimpleMonitor -- all confirmed byte-for-byte against the actual stream. A naive "fully inline all $ref pointers" JSON mode blew up to 516MB on DSC due to legitimate DAG sharing/back-references, so inlining is now memoized and gated behind an explicit --resolve flag; the default JSON keeps the graph as a flat objects table with $ref edges.

findings.evidence: tools/out/DSC_12G-HD.pkp.json: fully_parsed=true, bytes_consumed=629733, decompressed_size=629733; tools/out/DTP3_CP_42.pkp.json: fully_parsed=true, bytes_consumed=664380, decompressed_size=664380

findings.evidence: object id 124 (class StreamResourceAsset), members ResourceAssetBase+_key -> ref 23 -> 'extr_17_17677.py', ResourceAssetBase+_content -> ref 557 -> ArraySinglePrimitive Byte length 73045; decoded bytes start 'from Extron2.BaseDriver import BaseDriver' CRLF, 2136 lines, contains 'class extr_'. Same pattern in DTP3_CP_42.pkp.json object id 130, key 'extr_15_17578.py', content length 89571 bytes, 2326 lines.

findings.evidence: object id 125 (ClassWithId, metadata_ref 124), key ref 26 -> 'extr_17_17677_v1_0_0.pdf', content ref 565 -> ArraySinglePrimitive Byte length 333913

findings.claim: Per-device instance counts: DSC_12G-HD.raw has DriverCommandAsset=62, EnumStateAsset=890, DecimalParamAsset=137, EnumParamAsset=48, StringParamAsset=14 (param total 199), DriverModelAsset=1, DriverFileAsset=1. DTP3_CP_42.raw has DriverCommandAsset=96, EnumStateAsset=629, DecimalParamAsset=206, EnumParamAsset=123, StringParamAsset=21 (param total 350), DriverModelAsset=2, DriverFileAsset=1.
findings.evidence: class_instance_counts field in tools/out/DSC_12G-HD.pkp.json and tools/out/DTP3_CP_42.pkp.json

analysis.summary: The .pkp's structured NRBF metadata is a rich, independently-maintained object graph (DriverModelAsset, DriverCommandAsset, Enum/Decimal/StringParamAsset, EnumStateAsset, EthernetProtocolAsset, DanteAsset, StreamResourceAsset, UTF8Password, RevisionHistoryAsset) that overlaps heavily in naming with the embedded Python but is not simply a serialization OF the Python nor obviously the sole generation source for it. Field-by-field extraction shows the metadata carries information the Python cannot express (per-parameter min/max/suffix, connection/Dante settings, per-editor GUID change-tracking, a pointer to the embedded PDF comm sheet), while the Python contains substantial content the metadata schema has no room for (SIS byte-string templates, regexes, hand-written prose revision history and bug notes). Two concrete divergences across the two samples (a "ConnectionStatus" command asset with zero Python counterpart in DSC; five fully-implemented-but-commented-out commands in DTP3's Python that are still present as live-looking assets in the metadata) show the two artifacts can and do drift out of lockstep, arguing against tight, always-in-sync mechanical generation in either direction. The strongest reading is a hybrid/parallel-authoring model: metadata is the GC Designer's structured "property sheet" (edited via IDE UI, probably used to scaffold the command/parameter list), while the actual protocol logic in the embedded Python is hand-written/hand-maintained by the driver engineer and can be edited (including disabling buggy commands) without the metadata being correspondingly pruned.

findings.claim: Overall verdict on the decisive question: the evidence best fits a hybrid/parallel-authoring model, not a clean 'metadata generates Python' or 'Python generates metadata' pipeline. analysis.summary: Both embedded GC-runtime drivers (extr_17_17677 for DSC 12G-HD, extr_15_17578 for DTP3 CP 42) subclass Extron2.BaseDriver and follow one code-generator template with two literal, delimited regions per file — a hand-written/templated preamble+helper shell and an "### BEGIN/END AUTO GENERATION OF COMMAND DEF ###" block of per-command Set/Update/Match/Write/Read method quintets. The framework shell (parameter validation, __SafeToSet/__SetHelper/__UpdateHelper, status read/write helpers, StatusRefresh, Send/SendAndWait byte-encoding overrides) is provably byte-identical or near-identical between the two files by direct diff; several "universal" SIS commands (Firmware, MACAddress, SerialNumber) inside the auto-gen block are also byte-for-byte identical across both drivers. All device-to-driver communication is exclusively asynchronous: `self.Send()` writes a command string and a `re.compile()` regex registered via `self.AddMatchString()` parses the eventual unsolicited/echoed response — `SendAndWait` is defined (inherited override) but never actually invoked by either driver's command logic. There is no transport code (no socket/serial/SSH classes) in either embedded file; `configs['Interface']`/`configs['ConnectionType']` are opaque strings only inspected for an SSH-API-version gate, confirming BaseDriver (i.e., the closed-source GC runtime) owns the physical transport entirely. Quantitatively, the literally-shared scaffolding is roughly 300–360 lines per file (~14–16%), the labeled auto-generated command block is ~1660–1685 lines per file (~76–78%) and follows an identical method-shape template but with 0% shared literal text apart from a handful of universal SIS query commands, and the remaining ~180–260 lines are device-specific `__init__` registration data (Commands dict, AddMatchString regex list) plus, for the DTP3 matrix product only, unique local-state bookkeeping (`matrix_tie_status`, `matrix_io_names`) with no DSC analogue.

findings.claim: The GC-runtime driver therefore treats serial vs Ethernet vs SSH purely as opaque transport selected by the (closed) GC platform via the configs dict and BaseDriver.Send/AddMatchString — the driver author writes protocol-agnostic command strings and regexes and never touches sockets, which is a structurally different abstraction than the shipped ControlScript module (which explicitly imports and subclasses SerialInterface/EthernetClientInterface per the ground truth). This is a hard architectural divergence relevant to convertibility in either direction.

analysis.summary: Both shipped ControlScript modules follow one rigid two-class template: a device-specific `DeviceClass` (holding `self.Commands`, `AddMatchString` regex table, and per-command `Set*/Update*/__Match*` methods) plus a single transport mixin `SSHClass(EthernetClientInterface, DeviceClass)` — no other transport class (TCP/Telnet/Serial) appears in either file, confirmed by both comm-sheet PDFs which list "Supported Class and Example: SSHClass" / "Port Type: Ethernet (SSH)" as the only option. A ~170-line tail block (Set/Update dispatch, SubscribeStatus, NewStatus, WriteStatus, ReadStatus, `__ReceiveData`, AddMatchString, MissingCredentialsLog, and the SSHClass wrapper) is byte-identical between the two files except for whitespace, and is explicitly marked "RECOMMENDED not to modify the code below this point" — strong internal evidence it's a fixed template, not per-device code. Method bodies for commands are emitted in strict alphabetical order by command name (DTP3's Commands-dict order is itself alphabetical; DSC's dict has one out-of-order pair — Firmware before ExecutiveMode — while its method bodies are still strictly alphabetical), which is a generator fingerprint rather than a hand-authoring pattern. A SequenceMatcher line diff gives ~596 shared lines (48%/45% of the two files) concentrated in the 14 SIS status names both devices share (AudioMute, AutoImage, ConnectionStatus, ExecutiveMode, Firmware, Freeze, InputSignalStatus, Logo, MACAddress, OutputResolution, PowerSaveMode, SerialNumber, VideoMute, Volume) plus the identical framework tail; the remaining commands (15 DSC-only, 17 DTP3-only) are device-specific SIS logic.

analysis.summary: For the DSC 12G-HD, the .pkp's embedded GC-runtime Python and the shipped ControlScript module implement the same 29 SIS commands with byte-identical wire-format strings, value/enum maps, and response regexes in every case sampled except one (UpdateLogoAssignment). The Commands dicts differ by only 3 names total (PKP-only: UserDefinedCommand, UserDefinedString; CS-only: ConnectionStatus). A line-level diff (docstrings stripped, method names normalized) shows 74-81% of ControlScript's non-blank lines/characters appear verbatim in the PKP's embedded Python. The remaining ~20-25% is transport/lifecycle plumbing (socket transport class, receive-buffer/match-string loop, connection-heartbeat counter, Set/Update/SubscribeStatus dispatch tables) that GC's proprietary BaseDriver base class supplies invisibly and ControlScript must hand-implement from a generic, reusable-per-driver template - it is not device-specific and is not present as Python anywhere in the .pkp. Mechanical derivability of the ControlScript module's device-specific behavior is about 80%, with the caveat that every ported command still needs a spot-check against the SIS manual because at least one wire-string discrepancy (UpdateLogoAssignment) was found on direct comparison.

analysis.summary: For the DTP3 CrossPoint 42, the GC-embedded Python and the shipped ControlScript module implement the identical SIS wire protocol with near byte-identical per-command logic (tie-type maps, cmdstring formats, regexes, matrix-tie bookkeeping) — an ordered, comment/blank-stripped line match of 65% (706/1080 CS lines exactly match a pkp line in sequence), which is a floor since most non-matching lines differ only in mechanical ways (`_cmd_SetX` vs `SetX`, error-string wording). Command-set diff: 30 active pkp commands vs 31 CS commands; 3 pkp-only (MatrixIONameString, UserDefinedCommand, UserDefinedString — GC UI-only scratch parameters with no wire representation) and 1 CS-only (ConnectionStatus — connection bookkeeping); additionally CS still ships GlobalUSBDevicePort/USBDevicePort/USBOutputSignalStatus which the pkp's v1.3.0 revision-history docstring says were removed for firmware bugs, meaning the shipped CS module is frozen at an earlier (v1.2.0.0) release than the pkp source — a versioning/lifecycle divergence, not a logic divergence. The multi-model (USB variant) mechanism differs in *kind* but not in wire behavior: the pkp uses a real Python subclass `extr_15_17578_usb(extr_15_17578)` gated with `isinstance(self, extr_15_17578_usb)`, while ControlScript uses a flat `self.Models` dict of trivial setter closures selected by a `Model` constructor argument and gated with `self.ModelName == 'DTP3 CrossPoint 42 USB'` string comparisons — same decision points, different idiom. Matrix-specific state (nested `OrderedDict` mapping input→output→tie-state built in `UpdateAllMatrixTie`/`_cmd_UpdateAllMatrixTie`, and the plain-dict `matrix_io_names` cache) is structurally and byte-for-byte identical between the two, which argues that matrix complexity does not reduce mechanical derivability relative to the scaler case — it corroborates rather than breaks a scaler-based single-device conclusion. The framework-level gap is the same whole-class difference seen in scalers: GC's dual Live/Emulated status plumbing (`WriteStatusHelper`/`ReadStatusHelper`, `Mutex`, `ExtronTime`, `PostNewStatusEx`, `_cmd_SetSyncEmulatedStatus`, `_cmd_`-prefixed dispatch) is entirely absent from ControlScript's flat `WriteStatus`/`ReadStatus`/undecorated dispatch — a one-time, device-independent rewrite rather than a per-command judgment call. Net estimate: roughly 75-85% of the ControlScript module's command-specific logic is mechanically derivable from the .pkp (protocol constants, regexes, cmdstrings, and matrix-tie logic port essentially verbatim); the remainder is the fixed GC-framework-to-ControlScript-framework boilerplate rewrite (same every driver) plus per-driver judgment calls about which Emulated-only scratch commands to drop and which bookkeeping (ConnectionStatus) to add.

analysis.summary: Successfully extracted text from all 6 PDFs with pdftotext -layout (no missing-tool blockers). The two driver comm sheets (pkp and ControlScript, per product) enumerate command NAMES and enum VALUES that match the driver's internal Commands dict 1:1 (verified for DSC: 29-30 names line up exactly, and OutputResolution's ~70 enum labels match verbatim), but neither comm sheet contains a single literal SIS wire-protocol byte/string — they are UI-label documents, not protocol specs. The two product manuals DO contain real SIS ASCII command strings/response formats, but they document the FULL device protocol, a strict superset of what either driver implements (DSC: ~35 manual mnemonics tested, only 3 short/ambiguous ones plausibly present in driver code, the rest — Contrast, Brightness, Detail, H/V Shift, H/V Size, Auto Memory, Active Pixels/Lines, EDID mgmt, front-panel lock, logo file ops, unit/preset naming, factory resets — entirely absent from both the embedded GC python and the ControlScript module). Cross-referencing the manual against the driver also caught a concrete, high-confidence bug: the DSC embedded/pkp OutputResolution enum mislabels codes 59-66 as "3480x2160" (transposed digits; manual's numeric table says these codes belong to "3840x2160"), has a stray backtick in code '35`' for 1080i/50Hz (manual: plain '35'), and reuses code '59' for two different resolution labels — and this typo is baked into Extron's own shipped pkp comm sheet, not just the extraction. Separately, the manual documents Audio/Input Gain range as "-18 through +12 dB" while the comm sheet and the driver's own range check both use "-18 to 24" — a genuine three-way numeric conflict, not just a superset gap, showing the manual cannot be blindly trusted as ground truth either. PDF structure is highly consistent WITHIN each doc type across the two products (identical section skeletons: Device Specifications/Version History/Driver Notes/Control Commands & States/Status Available for pkp sheets; Device Specifications/Module Notes/Supported Class/Control Commands for ControlScript sheets; 4-column Command/ASCII-or-SIS-Command/Response/Description tables in both manuals), but column headers and the "Escape" symbol legend wording differ slightly between the two manuals, and naive linear-text extraction of the SIS tables produces inconsistent mnemonic tokenization (e.g., "ZPMAP" vs "Z"+"PMAP") that a real parser would need table-aware extraction to avoid.

analysis.summary: Going ControlScript .py -> .pkp is much harder than the reverse and is not just "brittle serialization," it is two stacked, mostly-undocumented problems: (1) porting the ControlScript code from the extronlib/DeviceClass runtime dialect to the GC-only Extron2.BaseDriver dialect, and (2) fabricating an entire proprietary NRBF asset graph (DriverModelAsset/DriverCommandAsset/ParamAsset/EnumStateAsset trees, ExtronCommandIdEnum IDs, schema/API version gates, integrity hashes) for which no schema documentation, and no visibility into GC's loader/validator, exists in the provided files. NRBF itself is not the blocker — it is a plain sequential, offset-free record stream (confirmed by walking real bytes), so a byte-accurate re-serializer is buildable in principle. The blocker is that GC's private "what fields must exist, with which exact enum integers, for the authoring UI and the driver-certification pipeline to accept and correctly render this" contract is invisible to us; several fields (_schemaVersion, _minAPIVersion, _resourceHashDict, ExtronCommandIdEnum values like 0 shared across dissimilar commands) point at validation/behavior we cannot observe or predict. The direction is answerable (I can say exactly what's missing and why) but I cannot say whether a hand-built package would load, and evidence suggests the practical use case is narrow to nonexistent for an outsider, since Extron's own filename/path metadata (an @Extron employee's OneDrive path, "Extron certified" wording) shows this is an internally-issued, certified numbering scheme, not an open one.

findings.claim: The embedded GC-runtime Python source is stored inside the .pkp's NRBF graph as a raw, length-prefixed Byte[] (ArraySinglePrimitive) member of DriverFileAsset — an opaque blob, not a structured/parsed representation. Its length matches the extracted .py file exactly.
findings.evidence: tools/out/DSC_12G-HD.raw byte offset 44730-44745: record bytes `\x0f-\x02\x00\x00U\x1d\x01\x00\x02` (RecordType 0x0f=ArraySinglePrimitive, PrimitiveTypeEnum 0x02=Byte) immediately followed by the literal text 'from Extron2.BaseDriver import BaseDriver\r\nimport re...'; decoded length 0x00011d55 = 73045 bytes, exactly equal to `wc -c tools/out/embedded/DSC_12G-HD.embedded.py` = 73045.
findings.implication: Swapping/writing the embedded-code blob is mechanically trivial (just a length-prefixed byte array, and NRBF has no absolute offset table so length changes don't corrupt other records) — PROVIDED you already have valid Extron2.BaseDriver-dialect Python text to put there. Building that text from a ControlScript module is itself a nontrivial rewrite (different base class, different Commands-dict shape, different imports per ground truth), so this only removes one sub-problem, not the hard one.

findings.claim: DriverCommandAsset is a rich structured type with 19 declared members including _exCmdId (type Extron.Configuration.Contracts.Enumeration.ExtronCommandIdEnum), CommandAssetBase+_attributes (DriverAttributeEnum), _internalName, _description, _groupName, _scriptName, CommandPacing, PollingInterval, and nested ObservableCollection<IParamAsset> — none of which have any counterpart in the ControlScript Commands dict, which only carries {'Parameters': [names], 'Status': {}}.
findings.evidence: tools/out/DSC_12G-HD.raw offset ~16100: class member-name list `_exCmdId, _extronName, _internalChildCollection, CommandAssetBase+_attributes, CommandAssetBase+_internalName, CommandAssetBase+_description, CommandAssetBase+_groupName, CommandAssetBase+_scriptName, ..., CommandPacing, PollingInterval` vs. samples/DSC_12G-HD/controlscript/extr_scaler_DSC_12G_HD_A_v1_0_0_0.py:24-50 where entries are e.g. `'InputGain': {'Status': {}}`.
findings.implication: A converter would have to invent values for every one of these fields per command (description text, group name, pacing/polling numbers, attribute flags) with no source in ControlScript to derive most of them from.

findings.claim: ExtronCommandIdEnum is a real .NET enum serialized with an underlying Int32 (`value__`), and a concrete observed instance value of 0 is reused via NRBF MemberReference across at least two functionally unrelated commands (LogoKeySetting and GlobalAudioMute), suggesting 0 is a generic/'no canonical ID' sentinel for driver-local commands rather than a per-command unique identifier — but the actual mapping table (which commands get a distinct nonzero canonical ID, and what integer) is not present or documented anywhere in the provided files.
findings.evidence: tools/out/DSC_12G-HD.raw offset 17923-18120: `...DecimalParamAsset...\x03\x82\xff\xff\xffExtron.Configuration.Contracts.Enumeration.ExtronCommandIdEnum\x01\x00\x00\x00\x07value__\x03\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00` (value 0) immediately preceding the string 'Logo Key Setting'; later at the same offset region the string 'Global Audio Mute' is preceded by `\x01r\xff\xff\xff\x7f\xff\xff\xff` (an NRBF MemberReference back to the same object, i.e. the same value 0).
findings.implication: If most custom commands can validly use exCmdId=0, that lowers the bar for many fields — but I cannot confirm whether GC ever requires nonzero canonical IDs for common capabilities (e.g. power/volume) to enable cross-driver UI features, since no such command was captured in the excerpts examined. Guessing wrong on the commands that DO need a specific nonzero ID (if any) is a silent-corruption risk, not a load-time error, since there is no signing/validation described that would catch a semantically wrong-but-structurally-valid enum value.

findings.claim: EnumStateAsset carries both a wire-protocol tag (_tag) and a separate GC-UI-facing display name (inherited AssetBase+_name/_defaultName) plus _validOperators (OperatorFlags) — i.e., GC driver states have two independent identities (protocol value vs. UI label) that ControlScript, which only encodes the protocol-facing regex/string mapping, does not preserve as a distinct structured property.
findings.evidence: tools/out/DSC_12G-HD.raw offset ~475052: class member list for 'Extron.Configuration.Core.Assets.Automation.EnumStateAsset' = `_validOperators, _tag, _internalChildCollection, AssetBase+_internalChildCollection, AssetBase+_defaultName, AssetBase+_name, AssetBase+_guid, ...`.
findings.implication: Recreating GC-facing UI text for every enumerated parameter state requires either the original human-authored labels or an ad hoc English generation from the protocol value (e.g. inferring '16:9' from a wire code) — not something recoverable from ControlScript source in general.

findings.claim: The .pkp filenames/internal names encode a two-part scheme: extr_<category>_<sequential> (17_17677 for a Scaler, 15_17578 for a Matrix Switcher), and the plaintext strings 'Extron', 'Scaler'/'Matrix Switcher', and the filename itself are stored as ordinary DriverModelAsset string fields immediately adjacent to each other — not as a separately-typed structured integer ID distinct from the string.
findings.evidence: tools/out/DSC_12G-HD.raw offset ~2350: `...\x06Extron\x06\x0c\x00\x00\x00\x06Scaler\x06\r\x00\x00\x00[C:\\Users\\billywong\\OneDrive - Extron\\Desktop\\pakage holding folder\\extr_17_17677_v1_0_0.pkp` ; tools/out/DTP3_CP_42.raw offset 2390: `...\x06Extron\x06\x0c\x00\x00\x00\x0fMatrix Switcher\x06\r\x00\x00\x00\x18extr_15_17578_v1_3_0.pkp`.
findings.implication: Nothing in the container schema itself forces the ID number to come from Extron's allocator — a self-chosen string like 'extr_99_00001' would be structurally legal. But the embedded build-machine path (an @Extron employee's OneDrive, 'pakage holding folder') and the comm-sheet wording 'Extron Certified' (samples/DSC_12G-HD/pkp/extr_17_17677_v1_0_0.pdf, Version History table) show these numbers are drawn from Extron's internal certification/allocation database, so a self-issued ID is not 'legitimate' in the shared namespace and risks future collision with a real Extron-issued driver of the same number.

findings.claim: DriverFileAsset/DriverDescriptorAsset carry explicit compatibility and integrity fields — _schemaVersion, _minAPIVersion, _fileVersion, _contentHashCode, and a package-level _resourceHashDict — none of which have any ControlScript analog.
findings.evidence: tools/out/DSC_12G-HD.raw offset ~300-450: member list `_manifest, _packageState, _resourceHashDict, _internalChildCollection, DriverDescriptorAsset+_fileVersion, DriverDescriptorAsset+_schemaVersion, DriverDescriptorAsset+_minAPIVersion, DriverDescriptorAsset+_manufacturerName, DriverDescriptorAsset+_deviceTypeName, DriverDescriptorAsset+_filename, DriverDescriptorAsset+_driverFolder, DriverDescriptorAsset+_contentHashCode, ...`.
findings.implication: The presence of explicit schema/minimum-API version fields strongly suggests GC performs some compatibility check on load, but whether it hard-rejects a mismatch, or what the hash fields are checked against, is unknown — I cannot inspect GC's loader. This is a real, named mechanism for GC to reject a hand-built package, distinct from (and not contradicting) the ground truth that there is no encryption or code signing: a content hash for change-detection/consistency is not cryptographic signing.

findings.claim: NRBF is a strictly sequential, length-prefixed record stream with no absolute offset table — confirmed by successfully walking real record boundaries (class defs, ClassWithId reuse, MemberReference, ArraySinglePrimitive) purely by reading length prefixes forward through both sample files.
findings.evidence: Multiple successful sequential reads in tools/out/DSC_12G-HD.raw and tools/out/DTP3_CP_42.raw, e.g. the DriverFileAsset class-member list at offset 322 followed immediately by its BinaryTypeEnum array and nested type names, and the ArraySinglePrimitive embedded-code blob at offset 44730 whose declared length (73045) exactly matches downstream content with no offset-table dependency.
findings.implication: This means NRBF's mechanical brittleness is about type-identity and exact member-name/order/BinaryType-tag matching per class (must match .NET's exact serialization contract for that assembly version), not about fragile byte offsets — a change in one field's length safely shifts everything after it. So a byte-accurate re-serializer is buildable with enough reverse-engineered class layouts; the risk is completeness/correctness of the semantic content (enum values, hashes, version gates), not the encoding mechanics.

## 1. Plain-English answer

Yes, for Extron's own SIS-based drivers this is possible, and it is much easier than the container format suggested at the outset. The .pkp is not a description of a driver from which code would have to be invented; it carries the complete driver as Python source (73,045 bytes in a StreamResourceAsset, JSON-DSC object 124, byte-identical to PKP-DSC), and that source shares its protocol logic with the shipped ControlScript module almost verbatim: 779 of 1,027 non-blank ControlScript lines (75.9%) appear word-for-word in the embedded Python for the DSC, and 706 of 1,080 (65.4%) match in order for the DTP3 (both figures independently reproduced by the verifiers). What differs is the runtime shell around that logic, and the shell is a fixed template: the last ~170 lines of the two shipped ControlScript modules are identical except whitespace (CS-DSC from line 1069 to end, CS-DTP3 from 1165). So a converter is a Python-to-Python transformation with a known target template, not a reverse-engineering exercise. What it cannot do is reproduce Extron's shipped modules byte-for-byte, because those modules are not a pure function of the .pkp (version skew, hand-edits, a dropped throttle, an orphaned command, all cited below), and it cannot prove the result works on a control processor without hardware.

## 2. What converts mechanically, and with what fidelity

The command block converts at near-verbatim fidelity. It is delimited in the embedded source by literal markers (`### BEGIN AUTO GENERATION OF COMMAND DEF` at PKP-DSC:178 and PKP-DTP3:326, `### END` at 1836 and 2011) and is 78% / 72% of each file. Within it, wire strings, value maps and regexes are the same bytes on both sides: `'w1*{}ASPR\r'` and `{'Fill':'1','Follow':'2'}` (PKP-DSC:182-236 vs CS-DSC:98-136); the AudioMute `OutputStates`/`ValueStateValues` maps and all three tag branches (PKP-DSC:300-366 vs CS-DSC:158-224); the 19-entry Logo map in identical key order (PKP-DSC:764-838 vs CS-DSC:386-441); the DTP3 `TieTypeStates = {'Audio': '$', 'Audio/Video': '!'}` and `'{}*{}{}'.format(...)` (PKP-DTP3:1191-1218 vs CS-DTP3:600-623); the entire OrderedDict matrix-tie reconstruction (PKP-DTP3:236, 289-322 vs CS-DTP3:176-201). Of 30 `AddMatchString` registrations in the DSC, 29 are character-identical; the one difference is `E(\d+)` vs `E(\d{2})` (PKP-DSC:162 vs CS-DSC:87). The `DEVICE_ERROR_CODES` table is byte-identical (PKP-DSC:1886-1900 vs CS-DSC:1036-1050).

The differences inside that block are regular and expressible as rewrite rules, which is what makes this mechanical rather than "mostly similar": `_cmd_Set<X>`/`_cmd_Update<X>` become `Set<X>`/`Update<X>` (PKP-DTP3:330 vs CS-DTP3:1167-1170 getattr dispatch on `'Set%s'`); `self.Write<X>(value, qualifier, 'Live')` becomes `self.WriteStatus('<X>', value, qualifier)` and the per-command `Write<X>`/`Read<X>` wrappers disappear (52 such defs in PKP-DSC, 44 in PKP-DTP3; CS files define only `WriteStatus`/`ReadStatus` at CS-DSC:1133/1158, CS-DTP3:1229/1254); the `if self.__SafeToSet('X'):` guard and the preceding `'Emulated'` pre-write are removed (PKP-DSC:190-196); `self.DriverCmd('UpdateAllMatrixTie', None, None)` becomes a direct call `self.UpdateAllMatrixTie(None, None)` (PKP-DTP3:218/228/230/233/861 vs CS-DTP3:111/119/121/125/455); handlers keep their `(self, match, tag)` signature (PKP-DSC:210 vs CS-DSC:116); and method bodies are emitted alphabetically by command name, which the shipped modules do even where their own dict order is not alphabetical (CS-DSC:30-31 dict has Firmware before ExecutiveMode; methods at 229/257/285 are sorted).

The Commands dict converts mechanically with one drop-list. The pkp dict entries carry `Set/Update/Live/Emulated` booleans plus `Parameters` and `Status` (PKP-DSC:48-77); the CS entries keep only `Parameters` and `Status` (CS-DSC:24-53). For the DSC, 28 names are shared, the pkp adds `UserDefinedCommand`/`UserDefinedString`, and CS adds `ConnectionStatus` (verified count: 30 pkp keys, 29 CS keys). `ConnectionStatus` is not a device command; it is written only from the template's `OnConnected`/`OnDisconnected` (CS-DSC:25, 1056-1062).

Model variants convert from metadata. The DTP3 .pkp has two DriverModelAsset instances whose names and script classes are exactly the strings ControlScript needs: object 127 `_name='DTP3 CrossPoint 42'`, `_scriptClassName='extr_15_17578'`; object 128 `_name='DTP3 CrossPoint 42 USB'`, `_scriptClassName='extr_15_17578_usb'` (JSON-DTP3, read this session). CS-DTP3:23-26 has `self.Models = {'DTP3 CrossPoint 42': self.extr_15_17578, 'DTP3 CrossPoint 42 USB': self.extr_15_17578_usb}` and the two trivial setters at 1156-1162. The pkp's `isinstance(self, extr_15_17578_usb)` (PKP-DTP3:229) maps to `self.ModelName == 'DTP3 CrossPoint 42 USB'` (CS-DTP3:120). One example only, so this rule is confirmed for one case and plausible in general.

The runtime shell converts by template, not by translation. `DeviceClass.__init__` state (CS-DSC:7-23), `__SetHelper`/`__UpdateHelper` (whitespace-only diff between the two CS files), and everything from the "RECOMMENDED not to modify" banner to EOF are device-independent; `SSHClass(EthernetClientInterface, DeviceClass)` with `__init__(self, Hostname, IPPort, Protocol='SSH', ServicePort=0, Credentials=(None), Model=None)` (CS-DSC:1217-1227) is copied, not derived.

## 3. What converts lossily, and what is lost

The GC dual-status model is dropped. `WriteStatusHelper`/`ReadStatusHelper` with `Mutex()`, `ExtronTime` timestamps and `PostNewStatusEx` (PKP-DSC:1945-2019), `_cmd_SetSyncEmulatedStatus` (2032-2062), `StatusRefresh` (2081), and the `ExtronTime(float)` tag class (2134-2135) have no ControlScript counterpart; grep for `Mutex|ExtronTime|PostNewStatusEx|_cmd_` over CS-DTP3 returns nothing. This is a clean drop because ControlScript's `WriteStatus` only tracks Live values, but any pkp code that reads Emulated state as an input is affected: `MatrixIONameCommand` pulls `number`/`name` from two GC-only scratch commands via `ReadMatrixIONumberSelect(None,'Emulated')` (PKP-DTP3:1051-1052), which the CS module turns into `qualifier['Number']`/`qualifier['Name']` (CS-DTP3:551-552) and a widened `'Parameters':['Type','Number','Name']` (CS-DTP3:46 vs PKP-DTP3:98 `['Type']`). The qualifier key names are a human choice.

Liveness and timing are replaced, not translated. The pkp arms a one-shot `CallBackTimer.Timer` as a response-timeout watchdog inside `_cmd_UpdateExecutiveMode` (PKP-DSC:432-438, `__ResponseTimeout` at 1906-1913) and gates the echo/verbose handshake on `'ExecutiveMode' == command` with `QueryDelayTimerIsRunning()` (PKP-DSC:1851-1876). ControlScript's template uses a `counter`/`connectionCounter=15` scheme in `__UpdateHelper` with `@Wait(1)` closures for the handshake (CS-DSC:995-1031). The observable behaviour (when a device is declared disconnected) therefore changes, and whether GC's BaseDriver behaves like the counter scheme is unknown (it is not in any file here).

Rate limiting is silently lost in Extron's own output. The pkp throttles `LogoAvailability` queries to one per 4 s with `time.monotonic()` (PKP-DSC:978-979) and validates the qualifier; the shipped CS-DSC:533-536 has neither, and neither CS file imports `time` (CS-DSC:3-5, CS-DTP3:3-6). A converter must choose between faithful (keep the throttle, add the import) and Extron-like (drop it); either way the result is not byte-equal to what Extron ships.

Documentation is lost. The pkp docstring carries the revision history and the bug notes that explain why five DTP3 commands are disabled (PKP-DTP3:38-43, 89-114 commented entries); CS files carry only a copyright line (line 1). The comm-sheet PDF travels inside the .pkp (JSON-DSC object 125, byte-identical to the on-disk PDF) and can be re-emitted but is not a .py concern.

Upstream defects propagate. The `'3480x2160'` transposition and the colliding code `'59'` exist in the pkp Python (PKP-DSC:1255-1263, 1291), the shipped CS module (CS-DSC:702-709, 743, 787-794, 828) and the pkp's own comm sheet (PDFTXT/extr_17_17677_v1_0_0.txt:136-138), while the manual's table says 3840x2160 (PDFTXT/68-3221-01_A_DSC_12G-HD_HD-12G_A_UG.txt:1991, 2028). A converter reproduces the bug faithfully; only a manual cross-check catches it.

## 4. What has no counterpart and must be hand-written or decided

Three things. First, the ControlScript runtime template itself for anything other than SSH: both samples ship `SSHClass` only (CS-DSC:1217, CS-DTP3:1313), `SerialInterface` is imported but only used in an `isinstance` check (CS-DSC:3, 1207), and both comm sheets list SSHClass as the only supported class. Serial/TCP/Telnet class bodies are unknown from these files and would have to come from other Extron modules or be written by hand. The transport choice is also not decodable from the metadata: the DSC EthernetProtocolAsset (JSON-DSC object 123) has `_port=22023`, `_SSHConnectionEnabled=False`, `_protocolSubType=EthernetTypeEnum=0`, internal name `'Ethernet'`, while the comm sheet says "Port Type: Ethernet (SSH), Default Port: 22023" (PDFTXT/extr_17_17677_v1_0_0.txt:321-322). The one mechanical source for "SSH" is the text of the comm-sheet PDF embedded in the package, which is a workable but fragile input.

Second, judgment calls that Extron's own output shows are made by hand: which GC-only scratch commands to drop (`UserDefinedCommand` actually sends bytes via `__SetHelper`, PKP-DTP3:1904-1908, so it cannot be dropped on a "no wire effect" rule; it must be a named drop-list), how to rename scratch reads into qualifier keys, and whether to keep throttles. Extron's own process is not clean here: CS-DTP3:48 declares `MatrixIONumberSelect` with no implementing method anywhere in the file.

Third, everything that depends on Extron's unobservable runtime: BaseDriver's `DriverCmd` dispatch, its polling loop that must be what invokes `_cmd_UpdateExecutiveMode` (never called from driver code), and the semantics of `StartQueryDelayTimer`/`QueryDelayTimerIsRunning`. The converter has to assume ControlScript's template equivalents are acceptable; that assumption can only be tested on a control processor with the device attached.

## 5. Proposed architecture

Hybrid, with the embedded Python as the primary source and the asset graph as the authority for inventory, naming and validation. Neither pure strategy works alone, and I want to correct the dossier on why.

Generating from metadata alone is impossible, but not for the reason the pkp-nonpython dimension gave. That dimension concluded the metadata holds no protocol information; on direct inspection it holds part of it. EnumStateAsset `_tag` is the wire token: `'Fill'` -> `'1'` (JSON-DSC object 2093, under param `Value` of Aspect Ratio), `'Audio'` -> `'$'` and `'Audio/Video'` -> `'!'` (JSON-DTP3 objects 2778/2779, param `Tie Type` of Matrix Tie Command), `'1'` -> `'01'` for HDCP Input Authorization inputs (matches PKP-DTP3:651-652). DecimalParamAsset carries ranges: Input Gain `_min=-18`, `_max=24`, `_suffix='dB'` (JSON-DSC object 1348, matching `if -18 <= value <= 24` at PKP-DSC:650); Volume `-100..0` (object 1345). What the metadata does not carry is command framing (`'w1*{}ASPR\r'`), response regexes, handler logic, or matrix bookkeeping, and some tags are empty (Matrix Tie Command Input/Output states have `_tag=''`). So metadata alone cannot yield a working driver, but it is a real cross-check for the value maps a translator lifts from code.

Translating the Python alone would work for the command block but leaves the converter guessing on model names and on the per-model command inventory; those live only in the DriverModelAsset tree (object 122 for DSC with a 31-entry command registry at object 1376; objects 127/128 for DTP3 with 29 and 31 entries, the USB model adding `USBInputSignalStatus` and `USBInput`). The per-model lists are also the correctly pruned ones: the five bugged DTP3 commands sit only in the file-level master list, not under either model (verifier finding, pkp-nonpython), so they can serve as the authoritative inventory.

Concretely, the pipeline is four stages. Stage 1, extraction: `tools/pkp_dump.py` already gunzips, parses every byte of both samples (`fully_parsed=true`, `bytes_consumed==decompressed_size`) and exposes the script bytes (object 124), the PDF (object 125), the model tree and the enum/decimal params. Stage 2, analysis of the embedded Python with `ast`: locate the class deriving from `BaseDriver`, the `self.Commands` dict literal, the `AddMatchString` calls, the marker-delimited command block, and per-command method groups keyed by the `<X>` suffix. Stage 3, transformation: apply the rewrite rules listed in section 2 (rename, unwrap `__SafeToSet`, delete Emulated writes and `Write<X>`/`Read<X>` wrappers, rewrite `Write<X>`/`Read<X>` calls to `WriteStatus`/`ReadStatus`, rewrite `DriverCmd` to direct calls, rewrite `isinstance(self, <scriptClass>)` to `self.ModelName == <model name>` using the metadata mapping, strip the four flags from each Commands entry, prepend `ConnectionStatus`, apply the drop-list, sort methods alphabetically), and flag for human review any `Read<X>(..., 'Emulated')` whose target is a scratch command, any `time.monotonic()` throttle, and any duplicate method definition (PKP-DSC defines `_cmd_SetUserDefinedCommand` twice at 1687 and 1693). Stage 4, emission: the fixed DeviceClass/SSHClass template with the transformed block spliced in, `self.Models` generated from DriverModelAsset names, and device-specific `__init__` state (`self.inputs`, `self.outputs`, matrix dicts, PKP-DTP3:135-137) copied through.

Verification should be semantic, not textual: extract from both the generated module and the shipped one the table of (command, cmdstring template, regex, value map, parameter list) and require equality, then report the residual diffs. On the two samples the expected residuals are exactly the known hand-edits (UpdateLogoAssignment PKP-DSC:919 vs CS-DSC:501; `E(\d{2})`; the LogoAvailability throttle; DTP3 version skew with the three USB commands live at CS-DTP3:355/925/938/943/1014/1022; the `MatrixIONumberSelect` orphan). A converter that reproduces everything else has done its job.

## 6. Effort and risks

The parser is done. The transformer is roughly ten AST rules plus a template and a comparison harness; with the two sample pairs as oracles, reaching "reproduces both shipped modules up to the documented residuals" is on the order of two to three weeks for one engineer who knows Python's `ast` well. That is an estimate, not evidence; the evidence is that the residual after mechanical rules is small and enumerable, which is what makes the estimate credible. Each new device family will cost extra whenever it exercises BaseDriver surface not seen here (`SendAndWait` is defined but never called in either sample; only one `Timer` instantiation per file).

Risk one is sample size. Two files, same generator, same vendor, both SSH-only. The parser's four hand-coded untyped NRBF shapes were reverse-engineered from these files alone and raise on anything new; the CS template for non-SSH transports is not in evidence; the runtime-apis dimension of the dossier was a placeholder (REFUTED), so no systematic BaseDriver-to-extronlib mapping exists beyond what I cited above.

Risk two is that Extron's shipped modules are not what the converter will produce, and reviewers will read that as failure. The DTP3 CS module is a v1.2.0.0 build while the pkp is v1.3.0 (filenames; PKP-DTP3:38-43 records the removal), the DSC modules differ by a hand-edit in UpdateLogoAssignment where the pkp version is the more broken of the two (it never references the Logo qualifier; the manual's `A X4# LOGO` syntax requires the slot number), and the throttle drop shows Extron simplifies when porting. Acceptance must be defined against the wire-string table, not the file.

Risk three is unverifiable runtime behaviour. Liveness, handshake timing and dispatch are replaced by template code whose equivalence to BaseDriver cannot be checked without a control processor and the device, and upstream data errors (the 3480x2160 table present in all three artifacts) pass straight through. A non-technical point outside the evidence but worth stating once: the output is a derivative of Extron-copyrighted code (CS-DSC:1 "Copyright 2026, Extron. All rights reserved.").

## 7. How the conclusion changes for third-party (non-SIS) drivers

The container side carries over intact: the NRBF schema is identical across the two samples, the script is an opaque byte array keyed by filename, and DriverModelAsset stores the manufacturer as a plain string (`_manufacturerName='Extron'`, object 122), so extraction of a third-party .pkp is expected to work unchanged unless it uses NRBF shapes the parser has not seen (it will raise rather than guess). The converter core also does not interpret the protocol: cmdstrings, regexes and value maps are copied as opaque data, so nothing in the section 2 rules is SIS-specific.

Everything else is unproven, and two parts are known to be SIS-specific in both artifacts. The handshake in `__SetHelper`/`__UpdateHelper` sends `'w0echo\r\n'` and `'w3cv\r\n'` and waits for `Vrb3`/`Echo0` (PKP-DSC:1851-1876, CS-DSC:88-89 and 995-1031); the error path matches `E(\d{2})` against an Extron error-code table; the heartbeat rides on `ExecutiveMode`. A non-SIS device cannot use that template, so both the pkp's shell and the CS template must look different for third-party drivers, in ways no file here shows. Third-party devices are also far more likely to be serial or plain TCP, which is exactly the transport class we lack. Whether third-party pkps use the same `### BEGIN AUTO GENERATION` generator and the same BaseDriver subset is unknown.

So the verdict narrows rather than flips: extraction, proven; command-block translation, probably portable but unproven; runtime shell, unknown. The right next step before any build is to obtain one third-party .pkp together with its shipped ControlScript module and run the same three-way comparison; without that pair, any estimate for the eventual target would be speculation.
